Neither my hon. friend nor myself is a lawyer, but I think I know that much about law. I will read a few paragraphs from the latter part of the decision:
Section 43 of the Immigration Act, which has already been several times referred to, is as follows:
"43. Whenever any person other than a Canadian citizen, or a person having Canadian domicile, has become an inmate of a penitentiary, gaol, reformatory or prison, the Minister of Justice may, upon the request of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization, issue an order to the warden or governor of such penitentiary, gaol, reformatory or prison, which order may be in the form F in the schedule to this act, commanding him after the sentence or term of imprisonment of such person has expired to detain such person for, and deliver him to, the officer named in the warrant issued by the deputy minister, which warrant may be in the form G in the schedule to this act, with a view to the deportation of such person."
If there is no authority in law for deporting the prisoner he must be discharged. If he is lawfully held for deportation the application for his release must be refused.
At the outset I was and still am of the opinion that the prisoner cannot be deported or held imprisoned for deportation for what I think is a rather obvious reason, viz: that his "sentence or term of imprisonment" has not "expired" within the meaning of the above section. Nothing that has happened for the purpose of accelerating his removal from the country can in my opinion have that effect. On this ground alone I think the prisoner is entitled to be discharged. However, the reasons upon which it is contended that the deportation is authorized by the act under the sign manual of His Excellency the Governor General will be given a fuller consideration. In determining the interpretation to be given to that document, it need hardly be said that the policy of the government as expressed therein in relation to the prisoner is immaterial except in so far as such policy can be legally implemented.
It is contended that the document is a conditional pardon. The right of the crown to grant a pardon subject to conditions is undoubted, but they must be lawful conditions and not repugnant to the pardon itself.
There is nothing on the face of the document I think to show that the prisoner's release is subject to any condition. It shows I think the purpose or motive of the release, and the legal consequences expected to follow therefrom, by
[Mr. WoodsworthJ
those on whose advice his excellency acted. But there is no question of a condition. The prisoner was to be released and nolens colons forthwith deported.
A word as to the powers of the crown in this connection is I think in order.
As I understand the law, a prisoner's sentence cannot be commuted, i.e., altered, except under the authority of an act of parliament; and this as I understand arises from the fundamental reason that sentences or terms of imprisonment are fixed by the courts in accordance with the law which is binding on the crown as well as the subject. In respect to sentence of death parliament has authorized such commutation. But such is not the sentence here. The "term of the imprisonment" referred to in section 43 means I think the term fixed by law for its duration and cannot in my opinion be altered at least against the will of the prisoner, for the purpose of accelerating his deportation. He has a right if he choose to take the limit of time allowed him before deportation. The crown in extending the royal mercy does not I think alter the law or the sentence or term of imprisonment fixed by law. In exercising this mercy by means of a pardon, the punishment is remitted but the sentence and period or term fixed for the punishment remain. If the prisoner is pardoned conditionally he has I think the right to refuse the pardon if he is unwilling to accept the conditions. If the prisoner has been pardoned (and I do not think he could be discharged from prison except in exercise of the power of pardon) he cannot in my opinion be deported. Freedom from deportation is incident to the pardon, because deportation was incident to the imprisonment. In any view' the prisoner is I think unlawfully detained for deportation and must be discharged.

From the decision
of Mr. Justice Mellish, published in the Halifax Chronicle of Monday, March 27, 1933. It seems to me that there are two points to be considered here. The first is that the so-called royal prerogative is being degraded. We have here a conditional pardon, a so-called pardon the outcome of which would be that the prisoner would receive a more severe punishment than that t.o which he had been originally sentenced. My next point is that if we are to maintain the dignity of the crown and all that goes with it we cannot allow matters of this kind to pass unnoticed. Further than that, it seems to me that the decision of Mr. Justice Mellish is a direct reflection on the Department of Justice. He says:
The right of the crown to grant a pardon subject to conditions is undoubted. But they must be lawful conditions and not repugnant to the pardon itself.
That is an implication that the conditions are unlawful, and under the circumstances I think the Minister of Justice should explain to this committee how his action was deter-

of his excellency under the royal prerogative to release for deportation, and it forms a complete answer to the argument now submitted to the committee by my hon. friend.

There are five confidential messengers provided for in this department. Will the minister give us some information in regard to this. My mind goes back to 192S when the present Minister of Justice was leader of the opposition in the House of Commons-	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Not in 1928.

In 1927. Although I
have not Hansard here to quote from, my recollection of the debate that took place then is that the then leader of the opposition made a very bitter comment on the fact that, there was one confidential messenger in the Department of Justice, and wanted to know what was the difference between a confidential and an ordinary messenger. Now we have five confidential and three ordinary messengers being provided for in the Department of Justice. What is the reason for the increase in the number of confidential messengers and what explanation has the minister to offer with regard to the salary that goes with the position? I would point out to him, what is obvious to everyone, that conditions in this
country in 1927 were very different from what they are now and if ever there was a time *when there should be a curtailment in the number of civil servants rather than an increase it is now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Without having the estimates for 1927 before me, I will guarantee that as between the estimates of that year and the present estimates there is a substantial decrease. I will also inform my hon. friend that the work of the Department of Justice has enormously increased, owing probably to the situation that exists throughout the country. In litigation there has been a very marked increase in the number of cases; our present prison population is up to 12,000, including penitentiaries and prisons; the number of opinions asked of the department are greater than ever before; and there is a very considerable increase in work and a very slight increase in staff. In the principal offices there has been a decrease. As regards the increase in messenger staff, that arises in part from the fact that the remission branch had to be moved from the east to the west block. I think one messenger is used between the penitentiary branch, which is in the Confederation block, and the east block. I think there are only two in that section of the Department of Justice over which I preside, one or two in the remission branch, and one or two, I am not sure which, in the Solicitor General's office. These are increases in minor offices and the salaries are set out at page 80, but there is generally a substantial decrease as between the estimates in the years 1927, 1928 and 1929 and the estimates now before the house.

Apparently the Minister of Justice thinks differently to-day from what he did in 1927, because in that year when he was leader of the opposition and the estimates of the Department of Justice were being considered-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not recall the incident.

I have a very clear recollection of it. The estimates contained a vote for one confidential messenger, and the then leader of the opposition, the present Minister of Justice, talked for about three quarters of an hour and wanted to know why the government-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I never do that.

He wanted to know the difference between an ordinary and a confidential messenger. He said that as far as he could see, a messenger who was a civil servant was a confidential servant of the gov-

eminent, and there could be no difference between an ordinary and a confidential messenger. The minister must have had a change of heart since that time, because he now offers estimates containing votes for five confidential messengers for the Department of Justice. It appears to me that there should be a curtailment of the number of employees in this department. If in 1927 the minister thought that one confidential messenger was useless and should not be employed, he should not come to the committee in 1933 with estimates for five confidential messengers. Is the business of government more confidential today than it was in 1927?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

One confidential messenger.

I have not forgotten. I remember well the discussion that took place at that time in the committee of the whole. There are one or two other observations I should like to make upon this vote. In 1927 when the minister was leader of the opposition, the Minister of Justice of that day had a private secretary. To-day the Minister of Justice has not only a private secretary but an assistant private secretary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have no private secretary; I save $4,200 there.

If I am in error I am
sorry.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends had better not laugh too soon. In 1927 the Solicitor General had a private secretary but in 1933 the present Solicitor General has a private secretary as well as an assistant private secretary.
And he has two additional ones down home.

I do not know about that, I am referring only to what appears in the estimates. Does the minister think it correct that the Solicitor General, who has always been considered a kind of fifth wheel

to the coach, should have a private secretary and an assistant private secretary? Are his duties such that he has to add to the civil service of this country? I am sorry the Solicitor General is not in his place but can the Minister of Justice defend this vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Before my hon. friend came into the chamber his leader raised this question and I explained it very fully. I have made inquiries with regard to the staff of the Solicitor General and I find that they are continually employed. The work in this department has more than doubled in the last three years. The Solicitor General is the only representative in the government from eastern Quebec and his correspondence is enormous. This matter was brought to my attention by the deputy minister and I have satisfied myself that the department is not overstaffed. I might give another instance in connection with the Department of Justice. At one time five lawyers were employed on the Soldier Settlement Board; these men have all been let out and the work is being carried on by the Department of Justice without any increase in staff.

I take it that the minister defends the increase from one to five in the number of confidential messengers, and defends also the Solicitor General having a private secretary and an assistant private secretary.
Do the estimates allow for the payment of salaries to private secretaries at the Soliticor General's home?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: None that I know of; I think they are all here.
Is the minister aware that the Solicitor General has two private secretaries at his service outside of the department?

Yes.

"Justice-salaries-to provide for salary of a confidential messenger, $1,200."

Simply because I have

speechtext: Immigration and Colonization-Immigration salaries and contingencies, $1,417,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister has been emphasizing in the last few days that the immigration work has dwindled down to next to nothing, that he is keeping out immigrants and not encouraging any to come in. I ask him how, in those circumstances,
does he justify asking for $1,417,000 for immigration salaries and contingencies outside of Ottawa, and outside of Canada altogether, I presume.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I do not think the right hon. gentleman is quite fair when he says that I have been stating time and again, or words to that effect, that no immigration is allowed to enter this country.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Well, boasting that it had been reduced to very little.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes, I think that is a fairer way of putting it. The type of immigration that my right hon. friend and his government permitted I have stopped, and I propose to keep on stopping it. Immigration that is now coming to Canada I trust is of a different calibre from a great number of those who were permitted to enter this country before 1930.
They will all be aristocrats, perhaps.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
No, hardly that. The outside service is mainly engaged in the patrol of the border and inspection at ocean ports. There is also a comparatively small expenditure in keeping open certain offices in the United Kingdom. I am told by the departmental officials that the boundary inspection work is now greater and more onerous than it has ever been in the history of the department. I am also told that on the United States side of the line, with the supervision of a population only as large as Canada's, the United States employ twice as many officers as Canada, doing the same sort of work. Each succeeding year new highways crossing the international boundary are coming into being. The tunnel and the new bridge at Windsor have also added slightly to the cost, although the committee will see that there is a decrease in the total vote. I am also told by the departmental officials that the reports and accompanying correspondence and also the general correspondence have very largely increased. I would point out to hon. members that it is very much easier to permit anybody to come into Canada than it is to select those whom you would like to have in this country, because there always arises the human equation in these matters, with pressure brought to bear on the minister and the government to depart from the rule in individual cases, and make departures sometimes from principles and policies as laid down. Those who have occupied the position of Minister of Immigration heretofore are well acquainted, I am sure, with the difficulties that are constantly arising in that connection.

How many offices in the United States has the minister closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: All of them.
How many have been closed in England? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There are just six offices open in England, three of them on part time, merely to keep the structure together and keep the contact alive, so that when we continue the work we shall not have lost the benefit of the organization that has been set up.
Is it still necessary to maintain officers on the continent? Do they do any examining there?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes. The situation that developed when the regulations were changed in 1930 was this, and it still prevails. Under the regulations as they then were and still are, the heads of families who preceded the family into Canada-I do not think it is possible to give the exact figures but they number very many scores of thousands-were permitted to have their wives and children follow them to this country, and that right of the head of the family in Canada was preserved in subsequent regulations. It is of course necessary to maintain the inspectional service, although that staff has been greatly cut down. For instance, there is not now an inspection service on the Baltic whereas formerly we had one at Danzig, but that has been closed. There is on the Atlantic coast and at Paris. In order to examine the wives and children and heads of families at present here, that service of necessity has to be continued, although with a reduced staff.

May I ask the
minister if he is still keeping one of those immigration officers at Father Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: So far as I am aware there never has been an immigration officer at Father Point.
Is there a medical examiner there?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The practice of the department has been to send an officer from Quebec to Father Point to board some of the larger steamers, in order to make civil and sometimes medical inspections.

But there is not
a station at Father Point?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.
Most of the continental examinations are made in Paris, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I think the major portion of it is done in Paris.

Where are the chief
immigration officers located in Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
London, Liverpool and
Glasgow.

Have you a full staff
at those points?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes, at those points.

Is the
Belfast office closed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Belfast is open.

May I bring to the attention of the minister the case of an immigrant named J. E. Flower who was brought to Alberta some years ago. I discussed this case with the minister last year. This man, with his family, wife and three children, was anxious to be sent back to the old country because he was not able to get any work in Canada which he could do. A year ago I took the matter up with the minister and, if I remember rightly, he informed me that if the province of Alberta could furnish railway transportation for the family to Montreal, it was just possible he might be able to have them returned to the old country. After the province agreed to furnish transportation to Montreal the minister said that before he could furnish ocean transportation somebody in the old country would have to signify his willingness to look after the man and family upon their return. Flower was unable to get anyone to guarantee to look after him. Finally, the provincial authorities, having grown tired of keeping the man and his family, advanced the necessary money to return them to the old country.
I have the following letter from the supervisor of charity and relief. Dated at Edmonton, September 3, 1932, it is as follows:
I am pleased to report to you that I have despatched this man and his family to the old country. The cost to the province, which Was paid from public funds, was $492, and I would appreciate it very much if you would use your influence with the federal government to have this province reimbursed for fifty per cent of the expenditure.
Oh, oh.

I say to hon. members that there is a very good reason why the federal government should assist in this case. The letter continues:
I have no record showing whether this man obtained an assisted passage, but from his statement on file he was unemployed in the

Supply-Immigration
old country and his father purchased transportation for himself rand family to Canada, and since his arrival here he has been a public charge. The province has already expended the sum of $2,381.50 for their maintenance.
Hoping that I may have a favourable report from your effort, for *which I wish to thank you in anticipation.
Yours truly,
A. A. Mackenzie,
Supervisor of Charity and Relief.
I wish to draw to the attention of the committee and the minister that this man and his family cost the province of Alberta a total of $2,873.50. That province had nothing to do with bringing him to Canada. At that time hon. members in this corner of the house were protesting against the government's immigration policy. The man in question had no employment in the old country, but his father paid for passages for Flower and his family to Canada. Alberta has spent, up to the present time, $2,381.50 for their maintenance, and is now paying $492 to ship them back to the old country, because it appears that they would be a charge upon the province as long as they remained in Canada. I admit the minister had nothing to do with bringing them to Canada, but the federal government has a responsibility. It seems to me unfair that the province of Alberta should have to pay $2,873.50 for one family.
How many years did that cover?
I think they came out in 1924. The circumstances I have outlined indicate the expense some of the western provinces have had to bear because of the immigration policy of the Ottawa government.
Address your remark to the hon. member for West Edmonton.

I am addressing my remarks to the Acting Minister of Immigration. I think in all fairness the government should share the expense of returning this family to the old country; that is ths least we could ask the government to do. I do not ask the minister to give me a statement offhand; I think he will remember our discussion of the matter last year. I hope at least he will promise to give the matter some consideration, and that the province of Alberta may hope to be reimbursed in part for the expense to which they have been put. It is most unfortunate that some of the provinces have to incur such heavy expenses because of an immigration policy carried out by a government
at Ottawa. At the time this family entered the country I believe the province of Alberta was not in favour of the immigration policy of the Ottawa government.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I have not a clear recollection of the case to which the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) has referred. Of course hon. members are well aware of the situation with regard to that and similar cases. Apparently the man and his family made legal landing in Canada, and complied with our laws as they then existed. I do not know whether they received any assistance from the British government when they came. But under the provisions of our law a person who resides legally in Canada for five years or more acquire domicile. Even if the Dominion government eared to invoke the provisions of the law with respect to deportation, we would be precluded from doing it by reason of his having acquired domiciliary rights. As to whether the policy of bringing immigrants into the western provinces has been beneficial, I have not much to say. I think the results were beneficial to the extent that desirable people were attracted to those provinces. Very great benefits resulted to the western provinces through the efforts of the Dominion government to procure desirable people for colonization within provincial boundaries. Our immigration law precludes the Dominion government from deporting- because that is really what it means-people who have legally landed in this country and resided here for five years. The five year period was thought by parliament to be long enough to indicate whether a person coming from other lands was a desirable citizen of this country or otherwise; I assume that is the reason the five year term was decided upon.
That places the British subject on the same footing as the foreigner, who could become naturalized in five years?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Yes. I had no authority
under the Immigration Act either to order a family deported on complaint of the municipality or province, or to pay anything with respect to the return passage. If the law were changed to cover cases of that kind I am afraid it would impose a very great burden on the treasury. I will admit that with respect to immigration we must of necessity take some chances; that is inevitable in the movement of people from the land of their origin to a country of adoption. I cannot but think that the western provinces have greatly benefited by the colonization of desirable people from other lands. There must
Supply-Immigration

be hundreds of thousands of that class. Of course there is a percentage of failures. It is a question whether the benefits should 'be set up against the disadvantages and the balance shouldered by the federal state. I do not think I would care to embark on any such bookkeeping; it would be hopeless.

Perhaps I should have said, if I did not, that this man had asked repeatedly for deportation. He wrote to me personally after he failed to interest the department. It was only because he wanted to be deported that I interested myself in the case. I would not ask that the man be deported if he did not himself desire it.

May I ask
the hon. member what was the matter with the family?

The man was unable to get work for a long period. Since he had been in the country, the province of Alberta had spent on relief for him and his family $2,381. It appeared that they would have to keep him and his family outright, for a good many years at any rate, and they paid $492 to send them back to the old country.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
When did the province
start to pay direct relief for this man?

I am sorry I have not got
that here, but I have read the letter from the officer in charge of relief at Edmonton giving the amount that the province had expended up to that time. The province thought it was much cheaper for the authorities to buy this man's passage back to the old country.

Was he
physically unfit?

He was a miner and his
eyesight was not good enough for him to get work in the mines. That is the only report I could get from the mounted police. He was located in a mining district and apparently there was nothing else for him to do. I want to urge this on the minister: He says we were taking chances on these immigrants. I think it is the province that took all the chance; the dominion did not take much. In this case the province had to take it all. If the man was on relief he would have to be kept jointly by the two governments, as I understand, because he was in unorganized territory outside a municipality and the Dominion government is just as much advantaged by this man being sent back to the old country as is the provincial government. If he were still here, if the province had refused to send him back, the province would

have had to keep him and his family, and the Dominion government would have had to share in the cost. If it was good business for the province to buy his passage back to the old country to save that unemployment relief cost for the next few years, surely it would be good business for the Dominion government to share in that expense. It seems to me unfair that the province should have to bear the whole cost. Under the circumstances I think it would be quite proper for the dominion to share in the cost of his transportation back.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: And apply the rule general!}'?
Well, I think so-apply the rule generally. I see nothing unfair to the dominion in that, but it is very unfair to the province as it stands at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: There has been some criticism in connection with a class of people against whom the municipalities and the provinces have made complaints and caused their return to their country of origin. I think perhaps the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) has been the most outspoken in that regard, with the possible exception of a newspaper or two. I put this to the members of the committee. If the suggestion of the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Coote) were adopted it would mean that people who have been in Canada for the time specified by the act for acquiring domiciliary rights, namely five years, or no matter how long ago they came to Canada say from Great Britain, should be deported, if through misadventure or through their own shiftlessness or through any other cause they are unable to support themselves in this country. Would it be fair to the United Kingdom that in those cases, after people had lived in Canada for perhaps ten or fifteen years, having made a legal landing in this country under our laws, the burden should be shifted back to the United Kingdom? My own view is that it would not be fair or just. There are cases like the one mentioned by the hon. member for Macleod which would seem to give some basis for action that might be taken jointly by the province and the dominion, but those cases are not very general, and I would not care to embark on the idea of making the general law conform to the particular case.

Whether it is made general or not, I feel that in this case, where the man asked to be deported-

But we could not deport
him.

He asked to be sent back;
what harm is there in advancing him the money and letting him go back? I think it would not be unfair to say that Great Britain has been relieved of his maintenance for possibly eight or nine years while he was in this country, so they would not object very seriously to having him back now. At any rate the province of Alberta thought it good business to pay his passage back rather than have him permanently on relief. They have thus relieved the dominion of a considerable burden of unemployment relief; why should not the dominion share in the expense of his passage to the old country where he wishes to go?

I think the hon. minister
means that if he paid the fare to return this immigrant it would be a precedent. I think he is right. I just want to ask a question; Is there any change in the Montreal office staff as compared with last year?

The salary Mr. Moquin used to receive?

speechtext: Yes.

In view
of whait the Prime Minister said the other day in regard to the tremendous importance of improving gold mining in Canada as a means of meeting tine present crisis, does the depart-

ment intend to assist prospectors in Ontario and northern Manitoba and British Columbia by airplane transportation and in other ways in order to open up new gold fields for production?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The question of government assistance to prospectors in Canada has been raised in a number of quarters at various times. I am sure my hon. friend is acquainted in some measure with the difficulties that beset us in turning the attention of people unacquainted with prospecting into that line of activity by reason of the very work in which they would have to be engaged. Prospecting for precious metals is a vocation that lends itself to but a very small percentage of our population. To be a prospector a man must have certain traits of character in perfect combination - characteristics that are not found in people generally. He has to be fearless, with abundance of courage; he must have patience; he must be a canoe man, a bush man, an axe man, a cook, and he must know how to travel with confidence in all sorts of country.
A jack of all trades.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
Much more than that. He has to know something about geology. Altogether, if there is one vocation in Canada, or for that matter anywhere in the world, that calls for a combination of faculties that are keenly alive, it is the game of prospecting. You cannot allow your courage to ooze out in that game or you will get nowhere. I quite appreciate that since the beginning of time great difficulties have faced every prospector -and I mean the good prospector, not the arm chair fellow-in even getting grubstaked to go out and investigate possibilities. That is one of the discouragements associated with tire effort, and even after he discovers some favourable ground that gives indications of valuable ore deposits he has only begun to meet the discouragements that are ahead of him, because he must be able to attract money in order to explore what he has found. There are so few who are able to measure up to the task that confronts the prospector that I greatly fear there would not be many who would be successful. Tiien there is the question of dealing with prospectors by way of assistance. I have thought it over a good deal and my own view is that the state had better keep out of that activity. I know the prospector about as well as anyone in this house and I know that he is a man who takes care of himself pretty well. He is not given to grumbling, and if the galleries in this chamber were full of prospectors I fancy there might

Sxipply-M ines
be some rather salty comments made upon some of the observations which we members of parliament utter at times. My own opinion now is, although I would not hesitate to give the matter further consideration, that this is an avenue which the state had better keep out of. If the state-aided prospector did find a gold mine or what afterwards developed into a mine, or if he found one of those rich little pockets where with a minimum of effort he captured from the ground say half a million dollars, how would you divide it? I think we should have a difficult time getting even the advance back. There are many barriers in the way of state-aided prospecting, and at the moment I would not favour it.
I agree in part with the minister, but I certainly must take exception to some of his remarks. In the first place, the government is aiding gold producers in Canada at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In what way?
By paying a premium in exchange to gold producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I disagree with the hon. member.

There are two arguments to be advanced. In the first place, if gold production is to be of fundamental importance in meeting our national crisis, then it should be encouraged in Canada. According to the Prime Minister's speech two or three days ago, the products of our gold fields were of great importance last year in helping to meet the situation, our gold production for that year having amounted to $63,000.000. My suggestion is this-and I am not putting it forward in any partisan sense but rather with the idea of being constructive. If gold is to remain the basis of our-currency in Canada, although personally I am strongly of the other view, I would point out that the gold committee of the League of Nations at the Genoa conference in 1920 predicted a decline in gold production in 1934 in the world stocks of gold, and if gold is going to remain as the basis of our currency I suggest that instead of the various forms of relief which the government is supporting at the present time the state should lend some assistance to the producers in proven gold fields. I think it would be a wonderful thing to assist the prospectors who to-day are unemployed in Vancouver and other cities, of whom there are hundreds, not amateurs but tried prospectors. They could be sent out with help from the dominion; the govern-53713-226
ment might provide them with four or five or six assistants and with a government engineer, if the department thought fit, so that they might go prospecting-that is, if the administration really believes that the accentuating of gold production values will be of benefit. Of course, if the administration does not believe in that, then my argument falls flat. At any rate, in the coming summer there is going to be a scurry in British Columbia to the gold mining prospects in the Cariboo and Bridge River country, and encouragement from the Department of Mines would be of great assistance to these men.

It is only recently that an effort has been made to prove or disprove an invention which it is said can produce iron at a profit from such ores. The government is always alive to the possibility of iron ores being found in Canada which can be converted by proper processes to the industrial uses for which they are intended, and in so far as finances will permit, the department will always be ready to make investigations with respect to such ores as may seem desirable in the premises.

This vote is to cover research and investigations by the Dominion Fuel Board and so on. Could the minister give the committee any information as to the activities of -this board in developing new uses for coal? I may be doing the board an injustice, but I do not think its efforts have been outstanding in this connection. I would draw the attention of the minister to a statement which has appeared in certain British papers to the effect that a new colloidal fuel has been developed. This fuel is a mixture of approximately sixty per cent coal and forty per cent oil. It was thought that it would be of great value to Canada because it would provide a cheaper fuel than oil and could be produced from Canadian coal. The inventor predicts its use in power plants requiring an intense -heat with the flexibility of oil fuel. There are a number of plants in this country that require an intense heat which does not go up and down such as coal heat. I would like to know if the fuel board has taken any notice of this development either by way of investigations of its own or in disseminating to the coal operators the results of the researches by the British and other governments and various universities. While I am on my feet I will ask the minister if his department is in possession of any information in connection with the use of oil developed entirely from coal. I notice that the British Admiralty has signed a contract with a company known as the Low Temperature Carbonization Limited, having factories in London and Yorkshire. It appears that the first bulk supply of this fuel is to be delivered to the destroyer Westminster and

it is expected that the ordinary cruising range of this ship with ordinary petroleum will be increased by the use of the new fuel without any adjustment of the standard equipment. The coal industry in the west, and possibly also in the east, is in a desperate condition and it would appear to be the duty of the fuel board to investigate any developments along these lines. Any information I have in this regard has been derived from sources outside of Canada and I would like to know what the fuel board has been doing in connection with the two items I mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The Dominion Fuel Board would have no connection with the matter to which the hon. member has referred. That board is purely administrative; its main work is in connection with the coal subventions, the determining of freight differentials and the allotment of competitive areas throughout Canada. I have heard from the departmental officers of the fuel developed by a combination of oil and very fine coal, and I understand that British chemists have made considerable advances with this fuel. Of course we have the benefit of what they are doing, just as they have the benefit of our investigations. I am sure the hon. member would not suggest that there should be a duplication of effort along these lines. This division has many activities. It has to do with the testing of fuel from every standpoint. It has been able to convince some of the large coking plants in Canada that they could use Canadian coal in their coking processes, the result being an increase in the use of Canadian coal.

That leads me to a discussion of the importations of coal into British Columbia from Great Britain. I regret that the departmental records do not seem to agree with each other. I have in my hand a letter from the minister's department saying that the importation of coal for the month of February was so much, but the figure does not agree with the records I get from the Department of National Revenue, and I take it that the Department of National Revenue is more likely to be correct because they actually collect the duty. The same thing occurred last year. I made a very definite statement as to the importations, and the minister contradicted my figures. He was perfectly sincere, but when we came down to analyze the thing we found that he was getting his figures from the Dominion Fuel Board and I was getting mine from the Department of National Revenue. They ought to agree, but they do not. It shows a little sloppy bookkeeping, that is all. However I want to deal with the importations of British bituminous coal into British Columbia. In the month of February last the imports were 2,244 tons, and in January 7,393 tons, making a total of 9,637 tons in two months. In previous years importations have been very small. In 1931 there were no importations and in 1932 only 1,100 tons. So it would appear that these importations are going up in a very marked degree, and it seems unfortunate when British Columbia coal production is going down.
I hold in my hand a record of production for the past month of February. The total production for Vancouver island in February of this year was 58,833 tons, against 75,787 for February 1932. That is a substantial reduction, running into nearly thirty per cent. The importation of British coal for the two months is equivalent to sixteen per cent of the production on Vancouver island for one month. We do not want to have our coal production cut down sixteen per cent, if we can possibly avoid it. I have no doubt the minister is familiar with the situation. I imagine it is the currency situation which enables coal to be brought out from England at practically ballast prices, and also in consideration of the British preferential arrangements which were made last summer.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No, that is not the major feature. The major feature is the operation of the Coal Mines Act in Great Britain, and the low ocean freight rates through the Panama canal to Vancouver. Of course the factors the hon. member has mentioned are contributory.

Does Britain subsidize her
coal mining?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.

Well then, that is unfair
importation; what about our dumping duty? In January the minister said: "I cannot say for the moment just what steps may be contemplated to deal with the situation". But I suggest it. is time some steps were taken. We cannot live in hopes of what is going to be done. I am not making my statement from a political standpoint at all. The minister may have observed that other hon. members from British Columbia and I have asked questions recently as to whether the Canadian National Railways purposed selling a large wharf they own in Vancouver harbour. It is well known that the suggestion is to sell it at a very low price. These are times when one can buy anything at a very small proportion of its cost. The suggestion is that a large importing company is going to buy the wharf with the buildings thereon for the purpose of establishing importations of British coal. The time to do anything towards checking such procedure is before an enormous investment is made, because if action is not taken immediately you are confronted with the necessity of dealing with vested interests. When we allow a trade to be built up, it is unfair to take steps to stop it after establishment. The time to act is before it reaches the stage of operation. When we are receiving 9,000 or 10,000 tons of coal in two months surely it is time for us to become alarmed, and especially when these importations are accompanied by heavy reductions in native coal production. I had hoped that the minister would take somewhat more drastic steps than simply to say the matter is before him. The matter may be before him two years from now.
While I am on my feet I should like to speak concerning another matter. In this connection I am not blaming his department. I notice that the importation of bituminous coal from the United States has increased enormously. In 1931 there were only 8,000 tons imported, in 1932, 5,000 tons, but in the month of February last alone, there were 2,413 tons. I cannot understand how it can be coming in in such increased volume, because we know the exchange situation makes it difficult for us to buy in the United States. If we are buying coal there, and they are competing with locally produced coal-

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Is that on the Pacific coast?

Yes, into British Columbia. It is remarkable that the amount should be in-

creasing in such large proportions. I cannot understand it, in view of the fact that exchange is decidely against such a trade. However, that is only a matter of comment. I should like the minister to assure us that he is taking some definite step, and that he is not only voicing an expression of good will in dealing with the importation of British coal. The other day the government promised immediately to put into effect the provisions of section 4 of the New Zealand treaty, which promptly put a check upon the importation of large quantities of New Zealand butter. Now is the time for us to take steps, before our local trade is ruined-it is badly handicapped now-and by the application of dumping duties, or some other means, apply a remedy.
The minister has advised us that the coal comes through the Panama canal bearing practically no freight charges at all, or only those charges which would apply to ballast. Then, apparently under the British Coal Mines Act the British industry is subsidized by the government. I suggest some very active steps be taken in the immediate future. I should like to hear from the minister.

There were 1,154 tons.
The matter of the importation of British bituminous coal has been before me, and I have been acting jointly and in cooperation with the coal operators on the St. Lawrence and on the western coast ever since the possibility of the importation of British bituminous in
any large amounts became a threat to the future markets for the Nova Scotia and the far western coal mines. It is a subject that the coal operators themselves, who are closely in touch with the situation, recognize as presenting difficulties. Only yesterday I spent a couple of hours with the heads of mining companies both east and west looking into the whole situation, in the hope that we ceuld find a solution which on the one hand would give the Canadian coal operators the home market, to which they think they are entitled,-and I do not disagree with them- and on the other hand refrain from placing on the consumer a burden which might in whole or in part be avoided. The question has not been so lightly regarded by me as the observations of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) would seem to indicate. I am not unacquainted with the difficulties that confront Canadian coal operators both in the east and in the west. There has been a very commendable disposition on the part of coal consumers to go a considerable way in using Canadian fuels even if they cost more than foreign fuels. There is a zone in Canada which I think the coal producers both east and west recognize that they cannot hope to invade with any degree of success. With respect to other sections of the country, we are making gradual but sure progress in the displacement of foreign fuels by Canadian coals. There has been the growing competition of oil, which tends J.o reduce the production of coal. That is a question that the producers are alive to, and we have discussed it with reference to the amount and the nature of assistance that the government may be able to extend to coal operators. I can only say what I have said before, that we are making headway. If the consumption had not fallen off, the provision that the coal miners themselves made by reducing overhead and increasing efficiency, combined with the assistance the government gave them, would have taken care of their requirements two years ago. But the mild winter of the year before last, and other factors, reduced the consumption, and we were again confronted with the difficulty of keeping our coal miners at work. Foreign fuels are a constant threat to the Canadian market. Hon. members of the committee are aware of the steps that the government has taken in an endeavour to conserve that market for our own producers as far as we economically can. Those efforts we shall continue to make, working in harmony with the coal producers. There is no movement of fuels into Canada that does not come under

Supply-Geological Survey-Coal
my review and is not discussed from time to time with the coal producers with the object of endeavouring to maintain those markets for Canadian producers. I am sure the hon. member must realize that the problem is a difficult and complex one. We have immense bodies of coal, but they are so located geographically that it is impossible to transport them economically in any considerable quantities into certain highly industrialized areas. There are markets that are available by reason of their geographical position, and in those markets, I am told by the coal producers, by the producers' own efforts and the assistance the department and this government can give them, we are displacing foreign fuels. The Winnipeg market is a striking instance, although foreign fuel has not been entirely supplanted there, and I doubt if it ever will be, having regard to various factors that enter into the question. At any rate I can assure the hon. member that the department has not overlooked any phase of this most complex question, and is working with the producers, endeavouring to lend such assistance as is justifiable.

With one exception the figures the hon. minister has quoted do not agree with those I got over his own signature from the Mines department. However, the differences are not very great, so I will not go into it. But I must certainly take exception to his statement that the importations into British Columbia of bituminous coal from the United States are steadily decreasing. He surely did not get the proper figures.

I have no figures prior to 1931. There is certainly a very disappointing increase in the present year. speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: What sort of action?

Put the dumping duty on. Do what you would do if the Toronto manufacturers came crying to you-get some action. The minister said that only a small amount of British bituminous coal had come in. Of course the word small is comparative, but it is not a fair word under the circumstances. The amount that came' in in 1932 was 1,154 tons-that is his own figure-and the amount that came in in the first two months of this year was practically 10,000 tons. I think those figures are occasion for some alarm-I got them from his own department. It is not a small amount when it is sixteen per cent of the output of the Vancouver mines for one month.
The minister told us he was glad to find that there was a disposition among coal consumers to pay more for the local product. But especially in these hard times-or in fact at any time-it is idle to appeal to the consumer on patriotic grounds to pay more than the market price. If he can buy cheaper somewhere else, especially in these hard times, when money is so scarce and every dollar has to be spread out to the utmost, he is not going to be willing to pay more than he has to. Any pressure of that kind has to be put on by the government in the way of taxation or bonus or dumping duty. He told us he was making progress with this problem. Yes, Mr. Chairman, we are making progress, but backward.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The producers do not think so.
It is not a matter of opinion. I would be quite willing to subordinate my judgment to that of the minister in a matter of opinion, but these are matters of cold, hard facts.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I will leave it to the producers.

The minister told us that the importation of bituminous coal from Great Britain in the year 1932 amounted to 1,154 tons, and he says that we are making progress now when we are importing almost 10,000 tons in two months. I do not know what kind of progress that is; it seems a retrograde movement to me, making haste backwards.
Then the minister introduced a feature that I had not commented upon; he said the consumption of coal, because of the hard times, was getting less. That makes the situation all the more acute, because I was not talking about the consumption but about the importation of coal. So if the importations are so

much greater and the consumption is so much less, it makes the situation even more acute than it was before. I suggest that it is about time we got away from expressions of sympathy, and saying, "We will have a conference about this." The law is there, and goodness knows we pay enough for the privilege of having it there. These dumping duties were imposed in 1930; they were going to protect the primary producer first, last and all the time, or at least that is what they were supposed to do. Now I am only asking that the law be invoked. I want some definite action; we should not wait until the house is burned down before considering what should be done about repairing the chimney in order to prevent a fire. Let us get some action before a trade is built up with a large vested interest which could not be thrown into the discard at a moment's notice without gross injustice. Ho not let the Britisher get a footing in that market, if you axe not going to allow him to have it permanently. That is not just to him, and it will only interfere with our relations under these conference agreements, which are putting us in rather a ticklish situation in some respects. We do not want friction in the future with Great Britain; let us take action now. We can take action against New Zealand; we could take action against Great Britain if it were a question of shirts or something like that. Let us take action now, when it is a question of the livelihood of the coal miners of British Columbia.
I should like the minister to explain the increase of $250,000 in this item.
They are having sympathetic meetings.

It was Colonel Villiers. He is in the city now, and the hon. gentleman can interview him and verify what I say. I am sorry I have not the correspondence before
me. The increase to which the hon. member for South Perth made reference has come about by reason of the increased movement under what are known as the coal subventions, and in large part by reason of the increase in the subventions themselves.
Just for my own information could the minister give me the amount of anthracite coal imported from the United States into Ontario last year and this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I am afraid that from the way these figures are tabulated I cannot give the complete picture. I can give the coal imported into what is known as the eastern zone. Apparently the trade has adopted certain zones for purposes of statistics; that is, they depend upon the laid down cost of the coal within a certain area.
What comprises the eastern zone?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
It comprises that part of Ontario east of a line drawn between North Bay and Kingston. The importations of anthracite into that zone for the past four years were as follows:
Tons
1929		 303,132
1930		 254,324
1931		 187,210
1932		 161,915
Does that include the whole of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: No.
I do not want to delay the committee. If the minister has not the figures would he be good enough to obtain them for me?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I should be glad to do so. The table is quite long and it would take some time to read it into the record, but I shall be glad to furnish the hon. member with a complete table showing the importations.
That will be quite satisfactory.

Some months ago an investigation was started into the importation of anthracite coal from Great Britain. -I should like to ask the minister when we may expect to receive that report, and whether we will get it in time to discuss it on the floor of the house if that should be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I believe that investigation will be concluded very shortly. It was not a simple matter, because I am beginning to learn that the coal business has many angles, and

Supply-Geological Survey-Coal
I can. easily understand that those conducting the inquiry had to go carefully into all the phases of the coal trade in eastern Canada. I hope, however, that the report will be ready perhaps within a week.

I would not want the coal producers and miners or the place which this great resource holds in our national life injured by my intervention in this debate, as the minister said was the case with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. Surely a member is entitled to express his opinion without having it suggested that his intervention is going to be injurious to the cause he is upholding. I do not think the minister does himself justice; perhaps he did not quite intend to say what he did. Certainly it does not give one a very good impression to have it indicated that a man who consistently advocates assistance to this industry is doing it harm. One can only think that the people who come to the government must be extremely careful of the company they keep, otherwise they will probably have a deaf ear turned to them. In spite of that I want to suggest one or two things with regard to what the minister has said. He made one of his usual extremely unctuous speeches, if I may say so without being offensive. He used the most general language possible, and if "apple sauce" is a permissible parliamentary expression it may be used to characterize the hon. gentleman's remarks. Some of his expressions were that people had shown a "commendable disposition" towards the use of Canadian coal; that he is "not unacquainted" with the difficulties of the industry; that he is "not overlooking" this great industry; that the government is endeavouring to give such assistance as would be justifiable", and so on. Now that does not sound very much like the member of a government led by a gentleman who gave the undertakings which his leader did to the coal industry in 1930. All over the province of Nova Scotia and particularly in the coal districts we were told definitely that there would be a national fuel policy, and nothing comes of it but a statement in 1933 that the hon. gentleman is not overlooking the situation. I suggest that it is time for the minister either to, fish or to cut bait, to tell us either that he'has a fuel policy or that he has not. In season and out of season I have done my best and stood abuse from this side of the house when I sat on the opposite side and was told that nothing was being done. I made no rash promises with regard to a national fuel policy, but endeavoured to do what seemed practicable and reasonable in connection with the industry; but this government 
came along with an entirely new proposition, namely, that the coal and steel industry should be benefited to the extent of the $55,000,000 that was going to the United States instead of going to the benefit of the people of Cape Breton-money that should be kept on this side of the line; but what they were led to expect has not materialized.
With regard to the dumping duties to which the minister has referred to-night, and which I have no doubt have been discussed with him in the lobbies of the house and in his office in the last day or two, the exchange dumping duty, as I understand it, is applied to coal at a low invoice price. The exchange dumping duty is being figured on so many shillings per ton, so that the fewer the shillings the less the duty and the less the assistance to the Canadian coal industry. I should think that the minister would be able to indicate to us whether it is intended to change that. God knows I am not in favour of this sort of duties, but if that is to be the policy let us have it all round and not some half hearted administration of it. If you are going to have a duty on everything else, if you are going to have irritating restrictions everywhere and a barbed wire on top of the fence, let us have it in connection with coal also and when the invoice value on everything else is raised do not let coal come in at nine shillings and sixpence when it is costing fifteen shillings at the port in England, and only charge the exchange dumping duty on that lower price.
With regard1 to other methods of assistance, I say to the minister frankly that I conratu-late him on the addition made to the maximum in connection with the freight subvention given to forwarding water-borne coal the year before last. But that does not appear to be producing the results which we were led to anticipate from all this talk about the national fuel policy. After so much talk about that policy my hon. friend should be able by this time, having been two years in power, to inform us either that he has some policy or that he has not.
Everyone knows that the coal situation is a difficult one; if it were not the coal industry would be in better shape to-day than it is.
. But it is because of these difficulties which my hon. friends opposite thought that they could solve that the industry is in such straits at the present time, and we feel that they should do something about it. If nothing can be done, then let the minister confess his inability in* the matter.
I would ask the minister to go into some detail with respect to the assistance furnished

the industry, particularly in the east. May I put to him these five questions: 1. How much coal was carried by freight subvention from Nova Scotia to Montreal all rail, last year?
2.	How much coal was forwarded by rail, after it had come by water to Montreal?
3.	How much coal was forwarded by water from Montreal to Toronto? 4. Is any extension of the fuel subvention area contemplated by the government this year? 5. Has the minister any additional proposals whereby he will promote assistance to the coal industry, particularly so far as the province of Nova Scotia is concerned?
These are things which the committee should know, and I submit that we should get along much better if the minister would tell us precisely what he intends to do to assist the industr3'. I do protest that it is scarcely the right thing for him to say that he is "aware of the difficulties," that he is "not overlooking" the industry, and that sort of thing. Instead of generalities, will the minister give us some definite information with regard to the eastern Canadian coal industry. Will he tell us what has been done during the last 3mar and compare that with the year before.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The total movement of coal from Nova Scotia last year was 711,589 tons, under the various subvention rates.
I should be glad if the minister would separate them.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I will endeavour to do so, although the figures are not compiled in that way. The all-rail rate in 1932, under order in council P.C. 1048, covered a movement of 15.854 tons. Under order in council P.C. 539, which covers rail and water rate, the movement totalled 59,667 tons. Under order in council P.C. 1300, rail and water rate, there were 214,085 tons.
Is that coal coming by water to Montreal and then forwarded inland?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is the rail and water rate. Under order in council P.C. 1048, for 1932, there were 39,847 tons.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is rail and water again.
We have to know the destination.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is to Montreal.
39,000 tons rail and water under P.C.1048-there must be a mistake when the minister says that is to Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is water to Montreal and then rail-*
Inland?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes.
What is P.C. 1300-the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: P.C. 1300 preceded P.C. 1048.
It covers the same thing?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The same thing. There were 74,196 tons under section 5 of P.C. 1048. Under section 6, there were 7,898 tons waterborne into Ontario through the canal system and then by rail to destination.
What is section 5?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I believe section 5 is waterborne west of Montreal; some of that coal would reach as far as Toronto.

P.C. 1300 and P.C. 1048
seem to be the same thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: P.C. 1300 preceded P.C. 1048. Under section 7 of P.C. 1048 there were 93,135 tons. Under order in council P.C. 944, there were 152,074 tons.
What is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That is coal for the Lasalle coking plant. If the hon. member desires, I will have a statement prepared covering all coal subventions.
What was the total for 1931?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines

speechtext: How much coal subject to the subvention did the Canadian National Railwaj's get?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That would be under order in council P.C. 1048. No coal was purchased by the Canadian National with the exception of about 10,000 tons at Taschereau and Cochrane.
How much of the coal bought by the Canadian National Railways was subject to the subvention?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: 7,562 tons.

The minister has stated that approximately 711,000 tons have been moved through these subventions. This was the total movement after the minister's announcement in the house last year that he hoped to promote the movement of an additional million tons of coal. That was broadcast all over Nova Scotia and when I asked

the minister about it, he used the same figure in the house. That statement was advertised very broadly in the government newspapers and when we are all through we find that not only has there not been an additional million tons of coal moved but the total movement under the subventions is approximately seven hundred thousand tons. I think I was right when I suggested that the minister has not shown in practice any benefits to be derived from the national fuel policy.
Progress reported.
